inner_core.name: Inner Core
inner_core.description: A solid ball of iron and nickel at Earth's center, nearly at its melting point despite the crushing pressure.
inner_core.about: Temperatures up to about {temperature} kelvin keep the inner core close to melting even under the weight of the whole planet. It turns slightly faster than the rest of Earth, which adds complexity to the magnetic field generated in the liquid layer above it.

temperature.source: NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, "A Guide to Cosmic Temperatures" (2023) -- Earth's inner core, a solid ball of iron and nickel about 1,220 km in radius, reaches temperatures up to 5,600 K. https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/14374/

inner_core.source: Dziewonski, A. M. & Anderson, D. L. (1981), "Preliminary reference Earth model", Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297-356; the model's tabulation, open: the appendix "The PREM Model", Table A.1, https://igpppublic.ucsd.edu/~shearer/ED2/appendices.pdf -- inner core boundary (ICB) at r = 1221.5 km.

outer_core.name: Outer Core
outer_core.description: A liquid layer of iron and nickel whose churning currents generate Earth's magnetic field.
outer_core.about: The outer core is molten iron and nickel with lighter elements mixed in, from about {top} kelvin where it meets the mantle to about {bottom} kelvin where it meets the inner core. Convection in this conducting fluid acts as a dynamo, the geodynamo, and produces the magnetic field that reaches out into space to form the magnetosphere.

top.source: Andrault, D., Monteux, J., Le Bars, M. and Samuel, H. (2016), "The deep Earth may not be cooling down", Earth Planet. Sci. Lett. 443, 195-203 -- sec. 4, p. 198: the core-mantle boundary temperature is at, or just below, the solidus of the silicate mantle, at 4100 (+/- 200) K. https://www.ipgp.fr/~samuel/henriIPGP/Publications_files/Andrault_etal.2016.pdf

bottom.source: Andrault, D., Monteux, J., Le Bars, M. and Samuel, H. (2016), "The deep Earth may not be cooling down", Earth Planet. Sci. Lett. 443, 195-203 -- sec. 3.3, p. 198: the melting point of pure iron at the inner core boundary, 6230 (+/- 500) K, lowered by about 650 K for the outer core's light elements, gives an inner core boundary temperature of 5580 (+/- 600) K. https://www.ipgp.fr/~samuel/henriIPGP/Publications_files/Andrault_etal.2016.pdf

outer_core.source: Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), PREM, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297-356; the model's tabulation, open: the appendix "The PREM Model", Table A.1, https://igpppublic.ucsd.edu/~shearer/ED2/appendices.pdf -- core-mantle boundary (CMB) at r = 3480 km.

lower_mantle.name: Lower Mantle
lower_mantle.description: The deep layer of hot, solid rock between the core and the upper mantle, flowing very slowly over millions of years.
lower_mantle.about: The lower mantle is solid silicate rock rich in iron and magnesium, under enormous pressure, from about {top} kelvin at its top to about {bottom} kelvin where it meets the core. Although solid, it creeps slowly by convection, and that slow flow is what drives the plates at the surface.

top.source: Katsura, T. (2022), "A Revised Adiabatic Temperature Profile for the Mantle", J. Geophys. Res. Solid Earth 127, e2021JB023562, doi:10.1029/2021JB023562 -- abstract: 1960 (40) K just below the 660-km discontinuity. https://d-nb.info/1271218135/34

bottom.source: Andrault, D., Monteux, J., Le Bars, M. and Samuel, H. (2016), "The deep Earth may not be cooling down", Earth Planet. Sci. Lett. 443, 195-203 -- sec. 4, p. 198: the core-mantle boundary temperature is at, or just below, the solidus of the silicate mantle, at 4100 (+/- 200) K. https://www.ipgp.fr/~samuel/henriIPGP/Publications_files/Andrault_etal.2016.pdf

lower_mantle.source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Earth, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html -- volumetric mean radius; Ishii, T., Huang, R., Fei, H. et al. (2018), "Complete agreement of the post-spinel transition with the 660-km seismic discontinuity", Sci. Rep. 8:6358, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-018-24832-y -- section "New results of the post-spinel transition pressure in complete agreement with the discontinuity depth": the global average depth of the discontinuity is 660 +/- 10 km.

upper_mantle.name: Upper Mantle
upper_mantle.description: The rock beneath the crust, including the partly molten layer where most magma is born and on which the plates slide.
upper_mantle.about: The upper mantle includes the asthenosphere, a partly molten layer that flows more readily than the mantle below it, letting the tectonic plates move. It reaches from the base of the crust down to the top of the lower mantle, at about {top} kelvin near its top and about {base} kelvin at its base.

top.source: Katsura, T. (2022), "A Revised Adiabatic Temperature Profile for the Mantle", J. Geophys. Res. Solid Earth 127, e2021JB023562, doi:10.1029/2021JB023562 -- abstract: on the adiabat the mantle is 1646 (35) K at a 50-km depth, 1994 (40) K just above the 660-km discontinuity, 1960 (40) K just below it, and 2587 (60) K at a 2,800-km depth. https://d-nb.info/1271218135/34

base.source: Katsura, T. (2022), "A Revised Adiabatic Temperature Profile for the Mantle", J. Geophys. Res. Solid Earth 127, e2021JB023562, doi:10.1029/2021JB023562 -- abstract: 1994 (40) K just above the 660-km discontinuity. https://d-nb.info/1271218135/34

upper_mantle.source: Dziewonski & Anderson (1981), PREM, Phys. Earth Planet. Inter. 25:297-356; the model's tabulation, open: the appendix "The PREM Model", Table A.1, https://igpppublic.ucsd.edu/~shearer/ED2/appendices.pdf -- base of the crust (Mohorovicic discontinuity) in the reference model, r = 6346.6 km.

crust.name: Crust
crust.description: Earth's thin, solid outer skin: the ground we live on, the ocean floors, and everything that has ever lived.
crust.about: The crust is thin compared with the planet: about {oceanic} km under the oceans, where it is mostly basalt, and about {continental} km on average under land, where it is mostly granite. The coldest temperature measured at the surface is {coldest} kelvin, at Vostok in Antarctica, and the hottest is {hottest} kelvin, at Furnace Creek in California. It holds all known life and every resource we can reach.

oceanic.source: NASA Science, "Facts About Earth" -- at the bottom of the ocean the crust is thinner and extends about 5 km from the seafloor to the top of the mantle. https://science.nasa.gov/earth/facts/

continental.source: NASA Science, "Facts About Earth" -- Earth's crust goes about 30 km deep on average on land. https://science.nasa.gov/earth/facts/

coldest.source: World Meteorological Organization, "Records of Weather and Climate Extremes" (table as of 31 July 2025) -- lowest temperature -89.2 degrees Celsius, Vostok, Antarctica, 21 July 1983. https://wmo.int/sites/default/files/2025-07/Table_Records_25Jul2025.pdf

hottest.source: World Meteorological Organization, "Records of Weather and Climate Extremes" (table as of 31 July 2025) -- highest temperature 56.7 degrees Celsius, Furnace Creek (Greenland Ranch), California, 10 July 1913. https://wmo.int/sites/default/files/2025-07/Table_Records_25Jul2025.pdf

crust.source: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet, Earth, https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html -- volumetric mean radius
crust.note: Drawn at the mean radius, the sphere the interior layers are measured against. The crust itself is too thin to show at this scale.
crust.radius_note: This is Earth's mean radius: the radius of a ball with the same volume as the smooth, slightly flattened shape fitted to sea level. The Earth radius used as a unit here is the equatorial radius, as the International Astronomical Union recommends, so the mean radius is a little less than one. The ground itself rises and falls from this by kilometres.

planet_radius.source: IERS Conventions (2010), Petit & Luzum (eds.), IERS Technical Note No. 36, Table 1.1, https://iers-conventions.obspm.fr/content/tn36.pdf

lower_atmosphere.name: Lower Atmosphere (to the stratopause)
lower_atmosphere.description: The air where weather happens and the ozone layer sits: the troposphere and stratosphere, holding nearly all the atmosphere's mass.
lower_atmosphere.about: The troposphere, on average the lowest {troposphere} km, is where clouds and weather form; above it the stratosphere, to about {altitude} km, holds the ozone layer. Together they hold more than {mass_share} percent of the atmosphere's mass, mostly nitrogen and oxygen. Temperature falls from an average of about {surface} kelvin at the surface to about {tropopause} kelvin at the top of the troposphere, then warms again toward the stratopause as ozone absorbs sunlight.

altitude.source: NOAA JetStream, "Layers of the Atmosphere", https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/atmosphere/layers-of-atmosphere -- stratosphere to about 50 km; and NASA, "Earth's Atmospheric Layers", https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/earths-atmospheric-layers-3/ -- the stratosphere extends to 50 km.

troposphere.source: NASA Science, "Earth's Atmosphere: A Multi-layered Cake" -- the troposphere extends from Earth's surface to, on average, about 12 km. https://science.nasa.gov/earth/earth-atmosphere/earths-atmosphere-a-multi-layered-cake/

surface.source: NOAA JetStream, "Layers of the Atmosphere" -- in the troposphere the temperature drops from an average around 17 degrees Celsius to -51 degrees Celsius at the tropopause. https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/atmosphere/layers-of-atmosphere

tropopause.source: NOAA JetStream, "Layers of the Atmosphere" -- the temperature is about -51 degrees Celsius at the tropopause. https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/atmosphere/layers-of-atmosphere

mass_share.source: UCAR Center for Science Education, "Demonstrating the Thickness of Atmospheric Layers" -- over 99 percent of the mass of Earth's atmosphere is in its two lowest layers, the troposphere and the stratosphere. https://scied.ucar.edu/activity/atmospheric-layers

upper_atmosphere.name: Upper Atmosphere (to the thermopause)
upper_atmosphere.description: The thin upper air where meteors burn up, the aurora glows, and the Space Station orbits, fading toward space.
upper_atmosphere.about: Above {stratopause} km lie the mesosphere, where most meteors burn up, the thermosphere, where the aurora appears and the International Space Station flies, and, higher still, the beginning of the exosphere. In the thermosphere the gas can reach about {thermosphere} kelvin, yet it is so thin it would feel cold to the skin.

altitude.source: NOAA JetStream, same page, https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/atmosphere/layers-of-atmosphere -- thermosphere from about 85 km to about 600 km, the exosphere beyond; NASA, same page, https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/earths-atmospheric-layers-3/ -- the thermosphere extends to 600 km.

stratopause.source: NOAA JetStream, "Layers of the Atmosphere", https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/atmosphere/layers-of-atmosphere -- stratosphere to about 50 km; and NASA, "Earth's Atmospheric Layers", https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/earths-atmospheric-layers-3/ -- the stratosphere extends to 50 km.

thermosphere.source: NOAA JetStream, "Layers of the Atmosphere" -- temperatures in the thermosphere can reach as high as 2,000 degrees Celsius near its top. https://www.noaa.gov/jetstream/atmosphere/layers-of-atmosphere

thermopause_low.source: UCAR Center for Science Education, "Layers of Earth's Atmosphere" -- the top of the thermosphere can be found anywhere between 500 and 1,000 km above the ground, its height set by how much energy comes from the Sun. https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/atmosphere/layers-earths-atmosphere

thermopause_high.source: UCAR Center for Science Education, "Layers of Earth's Atmosphere" -- the top of the thermosphere can be found anywhere between 500 and 1,000 km above the ground, its height set by how much energy comes from the Sun. https://scied.ucar.edu/learning-zone/atmosphere/layers-earths-atmosphere

upper_atmosphere.note: Drawn at a nominal top of {altitude} km. The real top, the thermopause, lies anywhere between about {thermopause_low} and {thermopause_high} km, rising and falling with the energy coming from the Sun.

geocorona.name: Exosphere / Geocorona (hydrogen halo)
geocorona.description: A faint halo of hydrogen gas that surrounds Earth and thins out far into space, the outermost trace of the atmosphere.
geocorona.about: The exosphere has no top: it simply thins into space. Its hydrogen glows faintly in ultraviolet light, a halo called the geocorona. The dots thin out as the hydrogen does. Out to {profile_to} Earth radii they follow a profile measured by spacecraft on the side facing the Sun: about {density} atoms per cubic centimetre at {density_r} Earth radii, a lower limit. Beyond {profile_to} Earth radii the measured rate of thinning is carried on outward, our choice for the picture. The hydrogen continues inward to the upper atmosphere, and it reaches beyond the Moon's orbit.

radius.hover_line: They stop at {value} Earth radii, about {km} km ({au} AU), where instruments lose the glow -- not where the hydrogen ends.

inner_radius.hover_line: The dots start at {value} Earth radii, about {km} km ({au} AU), where the measurements start.

Geophys. 40:271-279, https://angeo.copernicus.org/articles/40/271/2022/ -- sec. 6, eq. 7: the day-side hydrogen density fitted over the radial range 3-15 RE. Day and night: Zoennchen, J. Geophys. 40:271-279, https://angeo.copernicus.org/articles/40/271/2022/ -- abstract: the observations "constrained the neutral H density there at 10 RE to a value of 35 cm-3"; sec. 6: the "found value of 35 cm-3 at 10 RE is more likely to be a lower limit."

geocorona._declared: colour is a drawing choice. The exosphere is the stored drawing named under drawing: dots from inner_radius to radius, thinning as the measured profile does (to profile_to, then by its measured fall), drawn round, each shaded by its weight. The orrery places them and the page scales them by planet_radius and turns them to Earth's pole; how the dots look is a rendering setting in gallery/feature_renderers.js. Until 2026-10-17 it was a sphere shell at radius (L-292), with opacity, n_points and marker_size. L-410.
geocorona.source: Baliukin, I. I., Bertaux, J.-L., Quemerais, E., Izmodenov, V. V. & Schmidt, W. (2019), "SWAN/SOHO Lyman-alpha mapping: the hydrogen geocorona extends well beyond the Moon", J. Geophys. Res. Space Physics 124, 861-885, https://doi.org/10.1029/2018JA026136 -- the geocorona is detected to at least 100 Earth radii.
geocorona.note: Drawn round: the real hydrogen is denser near the line from the Sun to Earth, on both the day side and the night side. Only the shape of the thinning is drawn; a dot is not a count of atoms.

leo_inner.name: Low Earth Orbit, inner edge
leo_inner.description: The lower edge of low Earth orbit, the band of space where most satellites and the Space Station fly.
leo_inner.about: Low Earth orbit is the region from about {altitude} to {upper} km up. Satellites there circle at every angle to the equator, so together they form a shell around Earth rather than a ring, and each completes an orbit in about {period_low} to {period_high} minutes. The International Space Station, the Hubble Space Telescope, Starlink and most weather and Earth-observing satellites live here; the moving lights seen at dusk and dawn are usually these.

magnetopause.name: Magnetopause
magnetopause.description: The outer boundary of Earth's magnetic field, where it holds off the solar wind: pressed in by day, trailing a long tail by night.
magnetopause.about: Earth's magnetic field carves a cavity in the solar wind called the magnetosphere. On the side facing the Sun the wind presses it in; on the night side it stretches into a magnetotail observed far beyond the Moon's distance. The magnetopause is that boundary. It deflects the solar wind and turns aside many of the charged particles that reach Earth from the Sun and from beyond the solar system. The surface drawn is a model for a quiet solar wind; the real boundary moves in and out as the wind's pressure changes. In a strong storm the wind can push it inside the geostationary ring: on 21 January 2005 its nose came within about {storm} Earth radii of Earth's centre.

surface._model: Shue et al. (1998) eq. 10 with eq. 11. r = r0 [2 / (1 + cos theta)]^alpha, theta measured from the Sun-Earth line, r0 the standoff below. The flaring exponent is alpha = (a6 + a7 Bz)(1 + a8 ln Dp), with the paper's fitted a6, a7 and a8 (its Table 1), at the solar wind chosen for the picture.

bow_shock.name: Bow Shock
bow_shock.description: The shock wave where the supersonic solar wind first slows as it hits Earth's magnetic field, like the bow wave of a boat.
bow_shock.about: The solar wind moves faster than sound travels through the thin gas of space, so when it meets Earth's magnetic field it cannot flow smoothly around it: a standing shock forms upstream, sunward of the magnetopause, where the wind slows and heats. The surface drawn is a model for a quiet solar wind, and real crossings scatter around it.

surface._model: Jelinek et al. (2012), the paraboloid of eqs. 15-16 parameterised by tau: x = R0 p^(-1/eps) - tau^2 / 2, and the distance from the Sun-Earth line is sqrt(2 R0 p^(-1/eps)) tau / lambda. Where tau is zero this is the standoff below. A different functional form from the magnetopause because it is a different paper's fit, not a variation on Shue.

magnetotail.name: Magnetotail
magnetotail.description: Earth's magnetic field, drawn out by the solar wind into a long tail on the night side.
magnetotail.about: The solar wind drags Earth's magnetic field out behind the planet into a long tail. Spacecraft crossing it far downstream found that it stops widening about {flare_end} Earth radii behind Earth and is about {diameter} Earth radii across beyond there. ISEE-3 followed it out to {observed_extent} Earth radii, which is how far the spacecraft went rather than where the tail ends. The tail is drawn round, which is close to its shape on average; at any moment it is often flattened, in a direction set by the solar wind's own magnetic field, which keeps changing.
magnetotail._declared: The tail continues Shue's magnetopause surface from where the drawing of that surface stops, at the magnetopause's served cut angle; its starting distance and radius are worked out in the page from the served Shue rows, not served. From there it widens in a straight line to drawn_radius at flare_end, then keeps that radius to drawn_end, and it is round. flare_end and diameter are measurements; drawn_radius and drawn_end are rules over them, declared on their rows in constants_new.py, and the page uses them only for the shape. The five numbers the orrery's tail was drawn with until 2026-09-25 (100, 15 and 25 Earth radii, colour and opacity), which nothing in the gallery read, are gone (L-322 Stage D, gallery patch 3). color and opacity here are drawing choices, the magnetopause's, so the two read as one surface.

Koskinen and Kilpua (2022) sec. 1.1 put the outer reach at 7 to 10 R_E, which is why an outer figure near 10 R_E is not the physical impossibility one checker called it -- the belt's outer edge approaches the magnetopause, and magnetopause shadowing is a standard loss mechanism.

descriptions: A belt of trapped charged particles, mostly protons, held by Earth's magnetic field close above the atmosphere.
A broader belt of trapped electrons farther out, that swells and shrinks with solar storms.
abouts: The inner Van Allen belt is a region of energetic protons trapped by Earth's magnetic field. The particles are held along the field lines, so the belt curves down toward the ground on either side of the equator. The real field is tilted from Earth's axis and turns with Earth once a day; the belt drawn here follows the field's daily average, lined up with the spin axis.

The outer Van Allen belt is mostly energetic electrons, trapped farther out than the inner belt, and it swells and shrinks as the solar wind changes. Like the inner belt it is held along the field lines, which meet the ground nearer the poles; it is drawn around the field's daily average, lined up with the spin axis.

hill_sphere.about: Inside the Hill sphere a body can orbit Earth without being pulled away by the Sun. The Moon, about {moon} Earth radii away, lies deep within it. Beyond this sphere the Sun's gravity wins, and an object would drift into its own orbit around the Sun.

params.source: The pole the room draws is Earth's north pole on the scene's date from JPL Horizons (observer quantity 32, target 399), served by the cache builder as pole_of_date. The pole here is the FALLBACK, drawn only when no pole of date is served: the z-axis of the ICRF, which IERS Conventions (2010), IERS Technical Note 36, sec. 2.1.1, https://iers-conventions.obspm.fr/content/tn36.pdf, holds within about 0.02 arcseconds of Earth's mean pole at J2000.0, and which the Horizons manual's reference frames section, https://ssd.jpl.nasa.gov/horizons/manual.html, describes as aligned with FK5/J2000 to that level. The IAU working group report (Archinal et al. 2018) was cited here until 2026-09-26; it gives no pole for Earth and sends users to the IERS.

words._comment: L-421 (2026-10-06): the sentences the Earth room's drawn guides state about nature -- the axis, the Sun line, the terminator, the Moon's arc -- served here with their sources, because the guides are drawn from this block and the scene's moment rather than from a shell of their own. gallery/earth_geometry.js prints each hover as given; {name} is a value it fills in from the scene. Each guide's link is its entry's info_url: the axis's on sense, the Sun line's on subsolar, the Moon group's on moon_arc (chosen 2026-10-06, every one a URL a search returned that day; no NASA page is specific to any of the four, so each is its Wikipedia article).

sense.hover: The curved arrows at both ends show the sense of the turning: prograde, west to east, counter-clockwise seen from above the north pole.
sense.source: Sense of rotation: Archinal et al. (2019), Correction to: Report of the IAU Working Group on Cartographic Coordinates and Rotational Elements: 2015, Cel. Mech. Dyn. Astron. 131:61, doi:10.1007/s10569-019-9925-1 -- Fig. 1 caption: a body whose prime-meridian angle W increases with time rotates prograde. Earth's turning: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Glossary (consistent with The Astronomical Almanac 2023), https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/asa_glossary -- 'diurnal motion': the apparent daily motion of the sky from east to west is caused by Earth's rotation, so Earth turns west to east; 'direct motion': counterclockwise as seen from the north pole of the ecliptic, west to east -- the sense Earth's turning shares, so it is prograde. The two entries' wording is the Explanatory Supplement to the Astronomical Almanac's (Seidelmann 1992), checked against it 2026-10-06. The 2018 report (Cel. Mech. Dyn. Astron. 130:22) was cited here until 2026-10-06; its sections 2 and 7 were not re-read that day, so the citation moved to what was.

tilt_of_date.hover: Tilt: {tilt} deg on {date}, measured against the orbit of the Earth-Moon barycenter, the gravitational center of the Earth-Moon system, around the Sun that day (JPL Horizons).

tilt.hover: The axis slowly circles over thousands of years and nods slightly, so the pole and the tilt belong to that date.
tilt.source: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Glossary (consistent with The Astronomical Almanac 2023), https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/asa_glossary -- 'precession': the smoothly changing orientation of Earth's equator, driven by the Sun and Moon pulling on the equatorial bulge; 'nutation': oscillations of the rotation pole; 'true equator and equinox' of a date, which both affect. Williams (1994), Contributions to the Earth's obliquity rate, precession, and nutation, Astron. J. 108:711, doi:10.1086/117108 -- sec. 1 and 5: precession of about 50 arcseconds a year, one full circle in roughly 26,000 years. Both read 2026-10-06.

subsolar.hover: The dot where the line leaves the crust is the subsolar point, where the Sun is overhead.
subsolar.source: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Glossary (consistent with The Astronomical Almanac 2023), https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/asa_glossary -- 'sub-solar point': the point on a body's surface directly beneath the Sun, on the line from the body's centre to the Sun's; for a round body the Sun is at the zenith there. Read 2026-10-06.

terminator.hover:
The white circle is where the Sun is on the horizon: the sunlit half of Earth faces the Sun line, the night half faces away. The yellow line through the circle's centre is the Sun direction; its dot on the crust is the subsolar point, where the Sun is overhead.

FROZEN at {epoch}. The real terminator sweeps around Earth once a day; this scene does not turn. Geometry only -- no lighting is modelled, and the refraction and solar-disc corrections that define sunrise on the ground are not applied.
terminator.source: The terminator, 'the boundary between the illuminated and dark areas of a body', and the subsolar point: U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Glossary (consistent with The Astronomical Almanac 2023), https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/asa_glossary. Sunrise and its corrections: U.S. Naval Observatory, Rise, Set, and Twilight Definitions, https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/RST_defs -- Earth's rotation once a day causes rising and setting; sunrise is when the Sun's upper edge meets the horizon, its centre 50 arcminutes below it, 16 for the Sun's apparent radius and 34 for refraction. Both read 2026-10-06.

moon_arc.hover: The faint full ellipse is the same orbit swept once around; outside the arc, the Moon's real path drifts from it as the Sun and Earth's shape perturb the two-body orbit.
moon_arc.source: Williams (1994), Astron. J. 108:711, doi:10.1086/117108 -- sec. 1: strong solar torques drive the precession of the lunar orbit's plane, and Earth's oblateness adds a small torque; sec. 2: the lunar orbit is strongly perturbed by the Sun. U.S. Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department, Glossary (consistent with The Astronomical Almanac 2023), https://aa.usno.navy.mil/faq/asa_glossary -- 'osculating elements': the two-body orbit a body would follow if perturbations ceased. Both read 2026-10-06.
